title: Methods
text:
The experiment is located in the Jackson Demonstration State Forest in coastal northern California. Four harvest treatments were replicated at four sites in 2012: group selection (GS), high-density dispersed retention (HD), high-density aggregated retention (HA), and low-density dispersed retention (LD). The retained-overstory treatments targeted post-harvest relative densities of 13% or 21%; group selection created a 1-ha opening with a lightly thinned buffer. These treatments were designed to examine alternative pathways for developing multiaged redwood stands (Berrill & O’Hara, 2009; Reineke, 1933).
Ten years after harvest, regeneration plots and fuel transects were established within each 0.2-ha treatment macro plot. Regeneration measurements characterized redwood, tanoak, and Douglas-fir; fuel transects characterized dead surface fuels and live vegetation. The plots were remeasured after precommercial thinning, which released selected conifers from competing trees and shrubs.



Detailed sampling procedures, model diagnostics, and sensitivity analyses will be retained as supplementary material.


Basal area was modeled separately for redwood, tanoak, Douglas-fir, and other species using zero-inflated Gamma mixed models with a conditional log link. Treatment was a fixed effect; site and macro plot nested within site were random intercepts. Each species category had its own intercept-only zero and dispersion components. Each model used 64 vegetation-plot observations from four sites and 16 macro plots. Arithmetic mean basal area included modeled zeros and integrated over both fitted Gaussian random-intercept distributions. Confidence intervals for the means were calculated using the log-scale delta method with the full parameter covariance, including random-effect variance uncertainty. Redwood and tanoak estimates are displayed in the Results; estimates for all four categories are reported in the supplement.



Reported values are model-based arithmetic mean loads, including modeled zeros and integrating over fitted random effects, with equal weights for the four study-site contexts.
These estimates provide model-based reference means for comparable forest conditions; 95% confidence intervals were calculated using the delta method with the full parameter covariance, including uncertainty in random-effect variances. Mean woody standing-vegetation reduction was estimated as the pre-PCT minus post-PCT contrast from the matched repeated-phase model, with its joint covariance, and interpreted as a potential surface-fuel contribution.

text:
Discussion
The discussion will first interpret regeneration responses in relation to the silvicultural objective of developing a new redwood cohort beneath varying levels of retained overstory. It will then interpret phase-specific fuel conditions and the PCT-associated contrast as a linked management question, with conclusions limited to the reviewed sampling design and analysis.
This structure treats silviculture and fire management as linked management questions while keeping conclusions within the support of the reviewed analyses and cited literature.

title: Abstract
text:
Abstract
Forest managers using retention forestry need information on regeneration and fuel development to design productive stands in fire-adapted ecosystems. We analyzed 10-year remeasurement data from the Redwood Multiaged Experiment in Jackson Demonstration State Forest, California. The experiment compared group selection, aggregated retention, and low- and high-density dispersed retention treatments and measured regeneration, sprout growth, and surface fuel loading.
Redwood regeneration responded strongly to increasing canopy openness, whereas tanoak responses were more modest. Sprout-height findings will remain part of the main regeneration evidence. Fuel measurements describe conditions before and after precommercial thinning, including the PCT-associated contrast. The manuscript will evaluate how overstory retention affects regeneration while presenting fuel components in a form useful for integrated silviculture, fuels, and fire management.

write_publication_lines <- function(text, path) {
  connection <- file(path, open = "wb")
  on.exit(close(connection))
  writeLines(

To separate changes in models from changes in the prediction target, we’ll first reproduce means with random effects set to zero. These functions form equally site-weighted reference means and their standard errors for the later audit against integrated loads.

# rd04-reference-functions
# Keep valid nested identifiers from one observed row per site/treatment/phase.
# These identifiers do not contribute fitted random effects when re.form=NA.
reference_grid <- function(model, phase = NULL) {
  # Each site contributes once per treatment/phase, regardless of its number of
  # sampled corners or transects. Retain observed covariates such as zero-model site.
  keys <- intersect(c("site", "treatment", "phase"), names(model$frame))
  grid <- distinct(model$frame, across(all_of(keys)), .keep_all = TRUE)
  if (!is.null(phase) && "phase" %in% keys) {
    grid <- filter(grid, .data$phase == .env$phase)
  }
  counts <- count(grid, treatment)
  stopifnot(length(unique(counts$n)) == 1L)
  grid
}

# A maps row predictions to equally weighted site means. A V A' retains every
# cross-site covariance; treating site predictions as independent is incorrect.
averaging_matrix <- function(grid) {
  keys <- intersect(c("treatment", "phase"), names(grid))
  labels <- distinct(grid, across(all_of(keys)))
  # Stack one weight vector per target: rows are means, columns are grid rows.
  A <- do.call(rbind, purrr::map(
    seq_len(nrow(labels)),
    function(i) {
      keep <- purrr::reduce(
        purrr::map(keys, function(k) grid[[k]] == labels[[k]][i]),
        `&`
      )
      as.numeric(keep) / sum(keep)
    }
  ))
  list(A = A, labels = labels)
}

custom_reference <- function(model, grid) {
  # Response predictions include modeled zeros but set random effects to zero.
  # Their joint covariance is needed because site predictions share parameters.
  p <- predict(
    model,
    newdata = grid,
    type = "response",
    re.form = NA,
    allow.new.levels = TRUE,
    se.fit = TRUE,
    cov.fit = TRUE
  )
  avg <- averaging_matrix(grid)
  transform(
    avg$labels,
    estimate = as.vector(avg$A %*% p$fit),
    std.error = sqrt(diag(avg$A %*% p$cov.fit %*% t(avg$A)))
  )
}


For arithmetic mean loads across comparable sampling units, we need to average over the fitted random-effect distributions. We’ll extract the model matrices and full parameter covariance needed for exact integration. This calculation assumes independent Gaussian random intercepts and a log or identity link, so the function checks those assumptions before returning its inputs.


Code
# rd04-integration-setup
# Exact integration for THESE models: independent Gaussian random intercepts in
# the conditional model, log/identity link, no random effects in the zero model.
# This deliberately fails on slopes, correlated effects, offsets, or other links.
integration_setup <- function(model, grid) {
  vc <- VarCorr(model)
  # A 1 x 1 covariance at each grouping level identifies random intercepts only;
  # random slopes or random effects in other components need different integration.
  stopifnot(
    length(vc$zi) == 0L,
    length(vc$disp) == 0L,
    purrr::every(vc$cond, function(x) identical(dim(x), c(1L, 1L)))
  )
  X <- model.matrix(
    delete.response(terms(formula(model, fixed.only = TRUE))),
    grid
  )
  Z <- model.matrix(formula(model, component = "zi", fixed.only = TRUE), grid)
  # Match design columns to glmmTMB's parameter order before using its full
  # covariance, including covariance with the estimated random-intercept SDs.
  par <- model$fit$par
  ib <- which(names(par) == "beta")
  iz <- which(names(par) == "betazi")
  it <- which(names(par) == "theta")
  stopifnot(
    ncol(X) == length(ib),
    ncol(Z) == length(iz),
    length(it) == length(vc$cond),
    model$sdr$pdHess,
    isTRUE(all.equal(unname(par), unname(model$sdr$par.fixed))),
    is.null(model.offset(model$frame)),
    family(model)$link %in% c("log", "identity")
  )
  # Independent Gaussian intercept variances add on the linear-predictor scale.
  # Cross-check the reported variances against theta = log(SD) in the fit.
  variance <- sum(purrr::map_dbl(vc$cond, function(x) x[1, 1]))
  stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(
    variance,
    sum(exp(2 * par[it])),
    tolerance = 1e-8
  )))
  list(
    X = X,
    Z = Z,
    par = par,
    V = model$sdr$cov.fixed,
    ib = ib,
    iz = iz,
    it = it,
    link = family(model)$link,
    avg = averaging_matrix(grid),
    variance = variance
  )
}


With a log link, random-intercept variation changes the arithmetic mean. We’ll define the integrated means and their derivatives together for the uncertainty calculation. Identity-link means keep their original expectation.


Code
# rd04-integrated-means
# Independent analytic derivatives for the custom delta-method implementation.
custom_integrated <- function(s) {
  # s contains the prediction grid, fitted parameters, and their joint covariance.
  # ib, iz, and it locate the conditional coefficients, zero-model coefficients,
  # and log random-intercept SDs within that same parameter vector.
  # X %*% beta gives each grid row's linear predictor with random effects zero.
  eta <- drop(s$X %*% s$par[s$ib])
  # plogis converts zero-model log odds to the probability of a structural zero.
  # With no zero component, that probability is zero for every grid row.
  pzero <- if (length(s$iz)) {
    plogis(drop(s$Z %*% s$par[s$iz]))
  } else {
    rep(0, length(eta))
  }
  if (s$link == "log") {
    # For a mean-zero Gaussian random intercept b with variance v,
    # E[exp(eta + b)] = exp(eta + v/2), not exp(eta). Independent intercept
    # variances add, so s$variance includes every modeled intercept level.
    # Multiplying by (1 - pzero) includes the zero observations in the mean.
    # This exact integration concerns random effects, not Gamma residual noise.
    mu <- exp(eta + s$variance / 2) * (1 - pzero)
    # D is a sensitivity table: one row per grid row, one column per parameter.
    # Each entry is the derivative of that row's mean with respect to a parameter.
    # The delta method uses these slopes to propagate parameter uncertainty.
    D <- matrix(0, nrow(s$X), length(s$par))
    # Changing a conditional coefficient changes the mean by mu * its predictor.
    D[, s$ib] <- mu * s$X
    # A larger zero probability reduces the overall mean; the logit derivative
    # simplifies to -mu * pzero * its zero-model predictor.
    if (length(s$iz)) {
      D[, s$iz] <- -mu * pzero * s$Z
    }
    # glmmTMB stores theta = log(SD), so each variance is exp(2 * theta).
    # d(v/2)/d(theta_k) = exp(2 * theta_k); outer() applies this to every row.
    # These columns retain uncertainty in the integration multiplier itself.
    D[, s$it] <- outer(mu, exp(2 * s$par[s$it]))
  } else {
    stopifnot(length(s$iz) == 0L)
    # With an identity link, E[eta + b] = eta: mean-zero random effects do not
    # change the expected load. Only conditional coefficients enter its gradient.
    mu <- eta
    D <- matrix(0, nrow(s$X), length(s$par))
    D[, s$ib] <- s$X
  }
  # A forms equal-site means, or pre-minus-post contrasts after woody_change_setup.
  # Apply the same weights to the sensitivities to obtain the target's gradient G.
  G <- s$avg$A %*% D
  # Delta-method covariance = G V G'. V includes covariance between coefficients
  # and variance parameters, and keeps shared-parameter predictions correlated.
  # Dispersion parameters have zero derivatives because they do not enter this
  # expected-value formula. sqrt(diag(...)) gives each target's standard error;
  # pmax guards against tiny negative variances from numerical roundoff.
  list(
    estimate = drop(s$avg$A %*% mu),
    se = sqrt(pmax(0, diag(G %*% s$V %*% t(G)))),
    G = G
  )
}


The woody-change panel should describe the difference between the same means shown in the phase panels. This function forms pre-PCT minus post-PCT contrasts from the joint model, retaining their covariance for the uncertainty calculation.


Code
# rd04-woody-change
# Contrast the same matched model's integrated phase means, retaining their
# covariance through a single gradient and the full parameter covariance.
woody_change_setup <- function(s) {
  labels <- s$avg$labels
  stopifnot(
    all(c("phase", "treatment") %in% names(labels)),
    setequal(unique(as.character(labels$phase)), c("prepct", "postpct"))
  )
  treatments <- unique(as.character(labels$treatment))
  # Each contrast row selects one treatment's pre mean (+1) and post mean (-1).
  # All other treatment/phase targets receive zero weight.
  C <- do.call(rbind, purrr::map(
    purrr::set_names(treatments),
    function(trt) {
      stopifnot(
        sum(labels$treatment == trt & labels$phase == "prepct") == 1L,
        sum(labels$treatment == trt & labels$phase == "postpct") == 1L
      )
      as.numeric(labels$treatment == trt) *
        ifelse(labels$phase == "prepct", 1, -1)
    }
  ))
  # Compose contrasts with site averaging before propagating uncertainty, so
  # shared pre/post parameters contribute their covariance to the change SE.
  s$avg$A <- C %*% s$avg$A
  s$avg$labels <- data.frame(treatment = treatments)
  s
}


A second calculation will help us catch errors in the analytic derivatives. We’ll supply the same full parameter table to marginaleffects and compare its numerical delta-method calculation with the analytic route.


Code
# rd04-independent-delta-method
# marginaleffects does the nonlinear delta method on a supplied full parameter
# table, including theta (log SDs), not just the conditional fixed coefficients.
# avg_predictions(re.form=NA) alone does NOT integrate over random effects.
marginaleffects_integrated <- function(s) {
  # Supply ALL estimated nonrandom parameters, including log random-effect SDs.
  # The package's ordinary glmmTMB coefficient extractor uses fixef(), which
  # omits those SD parameters. Unique p1, p2, ... labels preserve their positions
  # despite repeated internal names such as beta and theta; V uses this order too.
  parameters <- data.frame(
    term = paste0("p", seq_along(s$par)),
    estimate = unname(s$par)
  )
  # A "functional" is simply a recipe mapping parameters to the means we want.
  # hypotheses() perturbs the supplied estimates and reruns this recipe to learn
  # its sensitivities numerically, independently of the hand-derived D above.
  functional <- function(x) {
    b <- x$estimate
    eta <- drop(s$X %*% b[s$ib])
    pzero <- if (length(s$iz)) {
      plogis(drop(s$Z %*% b[s$iz]))
    } else {
      rep(0, length(eta))
    }
    # Recompute v = sum(exp(2 * theta)) for EACH perturbed parameter vector.
    # Reusing s$variance here would hold the adjustment fixed and lose its
    # uncertainty. The formula integrates Gaussian intercepts exactly; only
    # the derivatives and the resulting delta-method uncertainty are approximate.
    mu <- if (s$link == "log") {
      exp(eta + sum(exp(2 * b[s$it])) / 2) * (1 - pzero)
    } else {
      eta
    }
    # Use the same site weights (or woody contrast weights) as the analytic route.
    # Return one estimate per target in the format hypotheses() expects.
    data.frame(
      term = seq_len(nrow(s$avg$labels)),
      estimate = drop(s$avg$A %*% mu)
    )
  }
  # fdcenter estimates each slope from small upward AND downward perturbations.
  # The package then combines those slopes with the supplied FULL covariance V,
  # implementing the same G V G' calculation as custom_integrated(). This checks
  # derivatives, not the shared model assumptions or choice of prediction grid.
  # Its default intervals are response-scale Wald intervals; the figure builds
  # positive mean intervals on the log scale later, using the audited SEs.
  marginaleffects::hypotheses(
    parameters,
    hypothesis = functional,
    vcov = s$V,
    numderiv = "fdcenter",
    conf_level = .95
  )
}

text:
07 - Audit prediction and uncertainty
Before using the estimates to describe fuel conditions, we’ll check that the calculation delivers the intended mean and interval. The audit below compares independent computational routes for zero-random-effect references and integrated means, including modeled zeros and equal site weights. Its tables show how integration changes the estimates and whether the routes agree on uncertainty, including uncertainty in random-effect variances. The F01 fits are held fixed throughout this check.
In the first table, model_id, component, phase, and treatment identify the fit and prediction target; n_sites counts the equally weighted sites. The remaining headings distinguish three ways to summarize the fitted model:

reference_* gives mean predictions with random effects set to zero; corrected_reference_se and marginaleffects_reference_se are their covariance-aware standard errors.
fitted_group_site_balanced_mean averages predictions using the sampled groups’ fitted random effects, first within sites and then equally across sites.
random_intercept_variance sums the fitted intercept variances on the link scale; integration_multiplier is the resulting mean adjustment, \(\exp(v/2)\) for log-link models and 1 for the identity-link difference model.
integrated_* averages over the fitted random-effect distribution. The custom and marginaleffects columns compare computational routes; integrated_se_* includes uncertainty in the estimated random-effect variances, and integrated_lcl/integrated_ucl bound the 95% confidence interval for the mean. Estimates, standard errors, and limits are in Mg/ha.

The second table records model formulas: conditional describes fuel load, zero the modeled probability of a structural zero, and dispersion the residual dispersion structure.


Code
# rd04-07-audit-rd04-inference
if (recompute) {
  publication_root <- normalizePath(getwd(), winslash = "/")
  paths_common <- publication_paths(publication_root)

  suppressPackageStartupMessages({
    library(dplyr)
    library(glmmTMB)
    library(marginaleffects)
    library(readr)
    library(tidyr)
  })
  models_dir <- file.path(publication_root, "outputs", "fuel", "models")
  audit_dir <- file.path(paths_common$output, "fuel/inference-audit")
  dir.create(audit_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

  # Read model identities from the current F01 register.
  spec <- bind_rows(
    filter(rd04_spec, !is.na(phase)),
    mutate(
      filter(rd04_spec, component == "Woody vegetation"),
      phase = "prepct"
    ),
    mutate(
      filter(rd04_spec, component == "Woody vegetation"),
      phase = "postpct"
    )
  ) |>
    mutate(
      component = sub(" fuel$", "", component),
      component = sub(" (pre-PCT only)", "", component, fixed = TRUE)
    )
  # Audit the signed alternative alongside the joint woody phase model.
  spec <- bind_rows(
    spec,
    transmute(
      filter(selection, response == "woody standing-vegetation reduction"),
      model_id = provisional_aic_leader,
      component = "Woody difference",
      phase = NA_character_
    )
  )

  audit <- list()
  structures <- list()
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(spec))) {
    item <- spec[i, ]
    message("Auditing ", item$model_id, " ", item$phase)
    model <- read_saved_model(
      file.path(models_dir, paste0(item$model_id, ".rds")),
      "F01"
    )
    phase_arg <- if (is.na(item$phase)) NULL else item$phase
    grid <- reference_grid(model, phase_arg)
    avg <- averaging_matrix(grid)
    reference <- custom_reference(model, grid)
    me <- as.data.frame(avg_predictions(
      model,
      newdata = grid,
      type = "response",
      by = intersect(c("treatment", "phase"), names(grid)),
      re.form = NA,
      allow.new.levels = TRUE
    ))
    me <- me[
      match(as.character(reference$treatment), as.character(me$treatment)),
    ]
    s <- integration_setup(model, grid)
    integrated <- custom_integrated(s)
    me_integrated <- as.data.frame(marginaleffects_integrated(s))
    # Require both implementations to agree on estimates and propagated SEs;
    # use the existing absolute mean and scaled SE tolerances for every fit.
    stopifnot(
      max(abs(reference$estimate - me$estimate)) < 1e-6,
      max(
        abs(reference$std.error - me$std.error) / pmax(1, reference$std.error)
      ) <
        1e-4,
      max(abs(integrated$estimate - me_integrated$estimate)) < 1e-6,
      max(
        abs(integrated$se - me_integrated$std.error) / pmax(1, integrated$se)
      ) <
        1e-4
    )
    # Verify integration at a point using numerical quadrature, independently of
    # the closed-form exp(v/2) calculation (including near-zero variances).
    if (s$link == "log") {
      quadrature <- integrate(
        function(z) exp(sqrt(s$variance) * z) * dnorm(z),
        lower = -12,
        upper = 12,
        rel.tol = 1e-9
      )$value
      stopifnot(abs(quadrature - exp(s$variance / 2)) < 1e-7)
    }
    # Check matrix construction against the model's own predict implementation.
    row0 <- if (s$link == "log") {
      exp(drop(s$X %*% s$par[s$ib]))
    } else {
      drop(s$X %*% s$par[s$ib])
    }
    if (length(s$iz)) {
      row0 <- row0 * (1 - plogis(drop(s$Z %*% s$par[s$iz])))
    }
    stopifnot(
      max(abs(row0 - predict(model, grid, type = "response", re.form = NA))) <
        1e-6
    )
    # Average ALL observed rows within site, then equally across sites; retaining
    # only one corner/transect per site would give an arbitrary conditional mean.
    observed <- model$frame
    if (!is.null(phase_arg) && "phase" %in% names(observed)) {
      observed <- filter(observed, .data$phase == .env$phase_arg)
    }
    conditional <- observed |>
      mutate(
        predicted = as.numeric(predict(
          model,
          observed,
          type = "response",
          re.form = NULL
        ))
      ) |>
      group_by(across(all_of(intersect(
        c("site", "treatment", "phase"),
        names(observed)
      )))) |>
      summarise(predicted = mean(predicted), .groups = "drop") |>
      group_by(across(all_of(intersect(
        c("treatment", "phase"),
        names(observed)
      )))) |>
      summarise(predicted = mean(predicted), .groups = "drop")
    fitted_groups <- conditional$predicted[match(
      as.character(reference$treatment),
      as.character(conditional$treatment)
    )]
    # Marginal mean intervals: log-delta intervals stay positive without truncation;
    # the signed identity-link difference uses ordinary response-scale intervals.
    lcl <- if (s$link == "log") {
      integrated$estimate *
        exp(-qnorm(.975) * integrated$se / integrated$estimate)
    } else {
      integrated$estimate - qnorm(.975) * integrated$se
    }
    ucl <- if (s$link == "log") {
      integrated$estimate *
        exp(qnorm(.975) * integrated$se / integrated$estimate)
    } else {
      integrated$estimate + qnorm(.975) * integrated$se
    }
    # Keep reference, fitted-group, and integrated targets side by side. The
    # fitted-group mean describes sampled groups; it is not the integrated target.
    audit[[i]] <- tibble(
      model_id = item$model_id,
      component = item$component,
      phase = item$phase,
      treatment = as.character(reference$treatment),
      n_sites = rowSums(avg$A > 0),
      reference_custom = reference$estimate,
      reference_marginaleffects = me$estimate,
      corrected_reference_se = reference$std.error,
      marginaleffects_reference_se = me$std.error,
      fitted_group_site_balanced_mean = fitted_groups,
      random_intercept_variance = s$variance,
      integration_multiplier = if (s$link == "log") exp(s$variance / 2) else 1,
      integrated_custom = integrated$estimate,
      integrated_marginaleffects = me_integrated$estimate,
      integrated_se_custom = integrated$se,
      integrated_se_marginaleffects = me_integrated$std.error,
      integrated_lcl = lcl,
      integrated_ucl = ucl
    )
    structures[[i]] <- tibble(
      model_id = item$model_id,
      phase = item$phase,
      conditional = deparse1(formula(model)),
      zero = deparse1(formula(model, component = "zi")),
      dispersion = deparse1(formula(model, component = "disp"))
    )
  }
  audit <- bind_rows(audit)
  write_csv(audit, file.path(audit_dir, "rd04-estimand-comparison.csv"))
  structure_path <- file.path(audit_dir, "model-structures.csv")
  structure_table <- as.data.frame(bind_rows(structures))
  write_csv(structure_table, structure_path)
}

The two routes agree closely on means and standard errors. Integration multiplies herbaceous means by about 2.0–2.3 and raises woody vegetation means by 33%, but changes duff by only 0.3%. Thus, the choice of prediction target matters most where fitted random-effect variation is larger; computational agreement alone does not establish model adequacy.
We’ll check the woody pre-minus-post contrast separately because its uncertainty depends on covariance between the two phases. The results below compare the joint-model calculation with the independent delta-method route, observed differences, and the direct Student-t model. This lets us inspect the consequences of the change-model choice while keeping the displayed contrast consistent with the phase means.


Code
# rd04-07-woody-contrast
if (recompute) {
  # A coherent mean change uses the same repeated-phase model on both sides and
  # its cross-phase covariance. Compare with the independently fitted t model.
  woody <- read_saved_model(
    file.path(
      models_dir,
      paste0(spec$model_id[spec$component == "Woody vegetation"][1], ".rds")
    ),
    "F01"
  )
  s <- integration_setup(woody, reference_grid(woody))
  s <- woody_change_setup(s)
  treatments <- as.character(s$avg$labels$treatment)
  change <- custom_integrated(s)
  change_me <- as.data.frame(marginaleffects_integrated(s))
  stopifnot(
    max(abs(change$estimate - change_me$estimate)) < 1e-6,
    max(abs(change$se - change_me$std.error) / pmax(1, change$se)) < 1e-4
  )
  # Descriptive observed change uses the same equal-site weighting as the target.
  # It provides context, rather than replacing the joint model's mean contrast.
  observed <- woody$frame |>
    group_by(treatment, phase, site) |>
    summarise(load = mean(load_mgha), .groups = "drop") |>
    group_by(treatment, phase) |>
    summarise(load = mean(load), .groups = "drop") |>
    pivot_wider(names_from = phase, values_from = load) |>
    mutate(observed_difference = prepct - postpct)
  # Signed changes can cross zero, so use response-scale Wald limits with the
  # joint-model SE; join the separate t-model estimate only for comparison.
  phase_change <- tibble(
    treatment = treatments,
    phase_model_difference = change$estimate,
    phase_model_difference_marginaleffects = change_me$estimate,
    se_custom = change$se,
    se_marginaleffects = change_me$std.error,
    lcl = change$estimate - qnorm(.975) * change$se,
    ucl = change$estimate + qnorm(.975) * change$se
  ) |>
    left_join(
      select(observed, treatment, observed_difference),
      by = "treatment"
    ) |>
    left_join(
      select(
        filter(audit, component == "Woody difference"),
        treatment,
        separate_t_model_difference = integrated_custom
      ),
      by = "treatment"
    )
  write_csv(
    phase_change,
    file.path(audit_dir, "woody-mean-change-comparison.csv")
  )
}

Some differences from the thesis may come from revised fits, and others from integrating over random effects. Code
# rd04-07-thesis-comparison
if (recompute) {
  # Read the thesis RESULTS grid already replayed and verified in the thesis
  # environment. This task uses that export without executing historical fits.
  thesis_reference <- file.path(
    paths_common$input,
    "fuel/thesis-reference-reproduction.csv"
  )
  thesis_results <- read_csv(thesis_reference, show_col_types = FALSE)
  stopifnot(file.copy(
    thesis_reference,
    file.path(audit_dir, "thesis-reference-reproduction.csv"),
    overwrite = TRUE
  ))
  lookup <- c(
    "1-hour" = "onehr",
    "10-hour" = "tenhr",
    "100-hour" = "hundhr",
    "1,000-hour" = "thoushr"
  )
  # Match only directly comparable deadwood classes, phases, and treatments.
  # The reference difference holds the zero-random-effect target constant;
  # integrated_custom separately records the effect of changing that target.
  comparison <- audit |>
    filter(component %in% names(lookup)) |>
    mutate(thesis_class = unname(lookup[component])) |>
    left_join(
      select(
        thesis_results,
        phase,

title: RD04 - fuel phase and PCT display
text:
Prediction and interpretation review
For the current display, we’ll use study-standardized, population-averaged expected loads: these include modeled zeros, integrate over the fitted random-intercept distributions, and equally weight the four study-site contexts. The historical zero-random-effect target remains a sensitivity reference. The fitted load models remain provisional pending scientific review.

What the prediction arguments actually do
In our fuel models, type = "response" includes modeled zeros, while re.form = NA sets random effects to zero and re.form = NULL conditions on fitted effects for known sampling units. Averaging these response predictions with marginaleffects does not integrate over random effects, and allow.new.levels = TRUE only permits new grouping IDs. RD04 instead integrates the response mean over all fitted Gaussian random intercepts, then averages equally across the four site contexts; this retains the fixed site effects in the post-PCT 100-hour model’s zero component (see the prediction documentation).


Thesis comparison
How much of the change from the thesis reflects a different fitted model, and how much reflects integration over random effects? We’ll collect all current fuel components and the historical references here, separating changes in the prediction target from changes in component definitions.
The thesis Results wrapper, marginaleffects_to_emmeans() in analysis/thesis/results.qmd, set re.form = NA for predictions and comparisons, using the default response scale and an equally weighted treatment-by-site grid for fuels. Converting these predictions to emmeans objects did not change their estimand. The original RD04 also used zero random effects and equal-site weights; its valid nested-ID grid gave the same standardization. Thus, differences between those references reflect fitted models and component definitions, rather than the choice of prediction software. Current RD04 adds random-effect integration while retaining equal-site weighting.
The 48 thesis references were reproduced from the saved fuel_tmb models in analysis/fuel_modeling_round_3.rda in the thesis environment and committed as an input export. Current references and integrated means come from F01’s saved publication fits. For deadwood, both eras use log-link Gamma models with a treatment effect and random intercepts for site, block, and corner within block; F01’s design_corner preserves the thesis corner grouping. Some zero and dispersion specifications changed: pre-PCT 1-hour removes the zero component and adds treatment-specific dispersion; pre-PCT 10-hour removes treatment terms from both components; post-PCT 1-hour removes treatment/site dispersion terms; post-PCT 100-hour adds their dispersion interaction; and post-PCT 1,000-hour adds treatment-specific zero probabilities. The other deadwood specifications are equivalent, although they are separate fits. Historical terms are recorded in analysis/analysis/fuel_modeling_round_3.qmd; current terms appear in the model-structure audit above. The F01 leaders remain provisional.
Only the four deadwood classes have matching component definitions. The thesis combined woody and herbaceous vegetation, combined pre-PCT litter and duff, and modeled a combined vegetation difference. We retain these historical rows alongside the separate current components and joint woody contrast, with their comparison status explicit. We do not repeat a combined thesis value against each separate component or treat a sum of separately fitted means as an equivalent historical fit. The separate Student-t woody-difference candidate remains in the earlier contrast audit; the table here uses the joint-model contrast chosen for the current display.
The table covers all four treatments, with loads and changes in Mg/ha. Fit change is the current zero-effect reference minus the thesis reference for matching deadwood rows; it includes refitting and specification differences, without isolating their individual effects. Integration change is the current integrated mean minus its zero-effect reference, holding the fit fixed. Total change is the sum of those changes for matching rows. Positive values indicate increases; these are point-estimate differences, not significance tests. Blank cells indicate that a counterpart or like-for-like difference is unavailable. The table also reports current integrated means and their 95% confidence intervals.
We’ll assemble this comparison from the saved audit and historical export on each render. Woody change uses the saved joint-model estimate and interval, with its zero-effect reference derived from the same model’s phase means. This combines existing results without refitting or recalculating inference.


Inspect all 76 thesis and publication comparison rows

  comparison,
  Component = component,
  Phase = dplyr::recode(
    phase, prepct = "Pre-PCT", postpct = "Post-PCT",
    difference = "Pre-PCT minus post-PCT"
  ),
  Treatment = toupper(treatment),
  `Comparison status` = comparison_status,
  `Thesis reference` = thesis_reference,
  `Current zero-effect reference` = reference_estimate,
  `Current integrated mean` = integrated_estimate,
  `95% lower` = integrated_lcl, `95% upper` = integrated_ucl,
  `Fit change` = reference_change,
  `Integration change` = integration_change,
  `Total change` = total_change
))







For matching deadwood definitions, the comparison separates fitting changes from the integration adjustment. Vegetation and forest-floor rows instead document changed component definitions. Neither larger means nor computational agreement establishes that a model is preferable.
The thesis Methods described averaging over random effects, but the Results code set them to zero. Its fuel estimates are therefore equal-site, zero-effect references rather than random-effect-integrated arithmetic means. For comparisons with other studies, we need to distinguish observed means, zero-effect references, and integrated means, as well as component definitions and sampling protocols. One unresolved provenance issue is the thesis Discussion’s approximately 42 Mg/ha of pre-PCT 1,000-hour fuel: the reproduced model references average 32.63 Mg/ha across treatments. The larger value needs its own source if retained.
The joint woody contrast represents a potential surface-fuel contribution, rather than measured slash deposition. The pre/post transition supports association with PCT; attributing all change to PCT requires additional design and time assumptions because these predictions have no contemporaneous unthinned comparison.


Integrated mean and uncertainty
For a treatment \(t\), phase \(h\), and equally weighted site contexts \(s\), define
\[
M_{th} = \frac{1}{4}\sum_{s=1}^{4}
  E_b\!\left[(1-p_{0,sth})\exp\{x_{sth}^{\mathsf T}\beta + z^{\mathsf T}b\}\right].
\]
The audited load models have independent Gaussian random intercepts only in the conditional model and no random effects in the zero component. Thus, with \(v=\sum_k\sigma_k^2\) across all modeled random-intercept levels,
\[
M_{th}=\exp(v/2)\,
\frac{1}{4}\sum_{s=1}^{4}(1-p_{0,sth})\exp(x_{sth}^{\mathsf T}\beta).
\]
Integration is exact under these fitted-model assumptions. Within a fitted load model, the common multiplier preserves treatment ratios and rankings while changing absolute loads and differences.
For uncertainty, we use the delta method with the full covariance of the conditional coefficients, zero-model coefficients, and log random-effect SDs, including their cross-covariances. For a target with gradient \(G\) and parameter covariance \(V\), its variance is \(G V G^{\mathsf T}\). This propagates uncertainty in the integration multiplier; scaling an old interval by \(\exp(v/2)\) would hold that multiplier fixed. The independent numerical check uses marginaleffects::hypotheses() with the same full parameter table and covariance.
Load means use 95% log-scale delta-method intervals to keep limits positive. Woody change uses the pre-PCT minus post-PCT contrast from the same joint model as the phase means, with their covariance retained. Its 95% response-scale interval can span zero. Separate phase intervals do not test a paired change, and inherited p-values or standard errors should not be carried over.
These are asymptotic confidence intervals for means, conditional on the chosen models and reference grid, not prediction intervals for new forests or transects. They exclude model-selection and fuel-component-derivation uncertainty. A refitted parametric bootstrap could assess the delta approximation, particularly for herbaceous loads with large variance corrections; that sensitivity analysis has not been performed.
For post-PCT 100-hour fuel, “site-standardized” retains an equal mixture of the four fitted zero-process site contexts. Random-effect integration cannot supply a zero-process coefficient for a fifth site. Generalization therefore requires comparable contexts and exchangeability assumptions. Four sites also provide limited information about the site-variance distribution. A regional or explicitly 50:50 aspect-standardized mean would require a justified target distribution and sufficient covariate information.


Methods wording
For the implemented population-average baseline:

We estimated treatment- and phase-specific mean fuel loads by averaging response-scale expectations, including modeled zeros, over an equally weighted grid of the four study-site contexts and analytically integrating over all fitted Gaussian random-intercept distributions. These estimates provide model-based reference means for comparable forest conditions; 95% confidence intervals were calculated using the delta method with the full parameter covariance, including uncertainty in random-effect variances.

The matched-contrast qualification can be stated in its own Methods sentence:

Mean woody standing-vegetation reduction was estimated as the pre-PCT minus post-PCT contrast from the matched repeated-phase model, with its joint covariance, and interpreted as a potential surface-fuel contribution.

)

  nrow(fuel_table_source) == 60L,
  !anyDuplicated(fuel_table_source[fuel_table_keys]),
  all(is.finite(as.matrix(fuel_table_source[c("estimate", "lcl", "ucl")]))),
  all(fuel_table_source$lcl <= fuel_table_source$estimate),
  all(fuel_table_source$ucl >= fuel_table_source$estimate)
)
fuel_table_rows <- unique(fuel_table_source[c("component", "phase")])
stopifnot(nrow(fuel_table_rows) == 15L)
fuel_table <- fuel_table_rows
for (trt in c("gs", "ld", "ha", "hd")) {
  # Require exactly one estimate per cell before rounding its mean and CI.
  values <- purrr::map_chr(
    seq_len(nrow(fuel_table_rows)),
    function(i) {
      cell <- fuel_table_source[
        fuel_table_source$component == fuel_table_rows$component[i] &
          fuel_table_source$phase == fuel_table_rows$phase[i] &
          fuel_table_source$treatment == trt,
      ]
      stopifnot(nrow(cell) == 1L)
      sprintf(
        "%s (%s, %s)",
        publication_number(cell$estimate),
        publication_number(cell$lcl),
        publication_number(cell$ucl)
      )
    }
  )
  fuel_table[[toupper(trt)]] <- values
}
fuel_table$component <- sub(
  " (pre-PCT only)",
  "",
  fuel_table$component,
  fixed = TRUE
)
fuel_table$component[fuel_table$phase == "Vegetation difference"] <-
  "Woody standing-vegetation reduction"
fuel_table$phase[
  fuel_table$phase == "Vegetation difference"
] <- "Pre minus post"
names(fuel_table)[1:2] <- c("Component", "Phase")
write.csv(
  fuel_table,
  "outputs/fuel/tables/rd04-fuel-display.csv",
  row.names = FALSE
)
publication_table(fuel_table)

Load means include modeled zeros, integrate over all fitted random intercepts, and equally weight the four study-site contexts. Woody reduction is pre-PCT minus post-PCT from the joint matched phase model, retaining pre/post covariance; it represents a potential surface-fuel contribution, not measured slash. Load intervals use the log-scale delta method; reduction intervals use the response-scale delta method. Intervals describe means, not individual observations, and exclude model-selection and component-derivation uncertainty. Models remain provisional. Post-PCT litter and duff are not estimated.

title: F01 - fuel-component separation and model exploration
text:
Original objective and guardrails
Create publication-only fuel components that preserve the thesis analyses while making the pre- and post-PCT data usable as distinct reference phases. During model fitting, retain the prescribed experimental-design random-intercept structure; record every model candidate and diagnostic; do not treat an AIC leader as a selected model.

Thesis notebooks, raw data, and thesis-era .rda objects remain unchanged.
Pre-PCT litter and duff are separated using the Finney–Martin model-3 forest-floor partition; post-PCT litter and duff are deliberately omitted because their boundary is not currently defensible.
Woody and herbaceous vegetation are separate in both phases.
The primary PCT contrast is matched-transect pre-PCT minus post-PCT woody standing vegetation - an inferred potential surface-fuel contribution, not a direct slash-load measurement.

The model comparisons produce more detail than fits comfortably on one screen. We’ll use a shared table formatter so readers can sort, search, and choose fields in the results below. Continuous estimates use consistent rounding, while AIC uses whole numbers to keep differences between candidates visible. Model identifiers use spaces in place of underscores in displayed tables so long names can wrap; saved identifiers retain their original spelling.

# f01-table-functions
# Show two significant figures, retaining trailing zeros below one and avoiding
# scientific notation. Round before formatting so large values are rounded too.
publication_number <- function(x, digits = 2L) {
  value <- trimws(formatC(
    signif(x, digits),
    format = "fg",
    digits = digits,
    flag = "#"
  ))
  value <- sub("\\.$", "", value)
  value[is.na(x)] <- NA_character_
  value
}

# Allow model identifiers to wrap without changing their saved values.
publication_model_id <- function(x) {
  gsub("_", " ", x, fixed = TRUE)
}

# Use the same controls for analytical results and CSV review tables.
# Keep the supplied order until a reader sorts, and escape data by default so
# formulas and HTML-like text remain literal. Integer counts stay exact;
# AIC uses whole numbers; other continuous columns use significant figures.
publication_table <- function(data, digits = 2L, caption = NULL) {
  model_ids <- names(data) %in% c(
    "model_id", "component_model_id", "provisional_aic_leader", "Provisional leader"
  )
  data[model_ids] <- lapply(data[model_ids], publication_model_id)
  if (!is.null(digits)) {
    numeric <- vapply(
      data,
      function(x) is.numeric(x) && !is.integer(x),
      logical(1)
    )
    aic <- numeric & tolower(names(data)) == "aic"
    data[aic] <- lapply(data[aic], function(x) {
      value <- formatC(round(x), format = "f", digits = 0L)
      value[is.na(x)] <- NA_character_
      value
    })
    data[numeric & !aic] <- lapply(
      data[numeric & !aic],
      publication_number,
      digits = digits
    )
  }
  DT::datatable(
    data,
    rownames = FALSE,
    escape = TRUE,
    caption = caption,
    extensions = "Buttons",
    selection = "none",
    width = "100%",
    options = list(
      dom = "B l f r t i p",
      order = list(),
      ordering = TRUE,
      searching = TRUE,
      scrollX = TRUE,
      pageLength = 10,
      lengthMenu = list(c(10, 25, 50, -1), c("10", "25", "50", "All")),
      buttons = list(list(extend = "colvis", text = "Show/hide fields"))
    )
  )
}

title: F01 - fuel-component separation and model exploration
text:
01 - Derive components and audit pairing
Before comparing treatments, we need fuel components that have a defensible meaning in each measurement phase. We’ll start by partitioning the pre-PCT forest floor into litter and duff with Finney–Martin model 3. The summary below shows the resulting loads and how often shallow-layer extrapolations needed to be bounded at zero. We’ll leave post-PCT litter and duff out because their boundary cannot currently be identified reliably.


Code
# f01-01-derive-components
if (recompute) {
  # Finney and Martin (1993), model 3: cumulative forest-floor mass (Mg ha^-1)
  # from the surface to depth ds_cm within a profile of total depth dp_cm.
  # The model is used only for the pre-PCT forest-floor measurements, where the
  # recorded total depth and estimated litter proportion describe the forest floor.
  # Its fitted range does not support a negative cumulative mass; the derivation
  # script records and bounds such rare shallow-layer extrapolations at zero.
  finney_martin_cumulative_load <- function(ds_cm, dp_cm) {
    result <- 6.461 * ds_cm^1.07 - 0.254 * dp_cm
    result[ds_cm == 0] <- 0
    result
  }

  publication_root <- normalizePath(getwd(), winslash = "/")
  paths_common <- publication_paths(publication_root)

  library(dplyr)
  library(readr)
  library(tidyr)

  paths <- publication_fuel_paths(publication_root)
  dir.create(paths$data, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
  dir.create(paths$manifests, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

  # Typed, checksum-validated exports from the separate thesis operation.
  transects <- readRDS(paths$input)
  legacy_total_load <- readRDS(paths$legacy_load_input)
  ids <- publication_fuel_ids

  # Keep the field measurements intact for audit. Post-PCT forest-floor values
  # are retained here but deliberately receive no duff/litter load conversion.
  forest_floor_station <- transects |>
    select(phase, all_of(ids), matches("^(duff_litter|pct_litter|fbd)[12]$")) |>
    pivot_longer(
      cols = matches("^(duff_litter|pct_litter|fbd)[12]$"),
      names_to = c(".value", "station"),
      names_pattern = "(.*?)([12])$"
    ) |>
    transmute(
      phase,
      across(all_of(ids)),
      station = as.integer(station),
      total_forest_floor_depth_cm = duff_litter,
      estimated_litter_fraction = pct_litter / 100,
      estimated_litter_depth_cm = total_forest_floor_depth_cm *
        estimated_litter_fraction,
      estimated_duff_depth_cm = total_forest_floor_depth_cm -
        estimated_litter_depth_cm,
      fuel_bed_depth_cm = fbd,
      forest_floor_load_eligible = phase == "prepct"
    )

  if (
    any(
      forest_floor_station$estimated_litter_fraction < 0 |
        forest_floor_station$estimated_litter_fraction > 1,
      na.rm = TRUE
    )
  ) {
    stop("Estimated litter fractions fall outside [0, 1].")
  }

  # Finney and Martin's cumulative curve partitions the pre-PCT total profile at
  # the estimated litter/duff boundary. These are model-derived loads, not direct
  # independent bulk-density measurements of the two layers.
  forest_floor_pre_station <- forest_floor_station |>
    filter(forest_floor_load_eligible) |>
    mutate(
      total_forest_floor_load_mgha = finney_martin_cumulative_load(
        total_forest_floor_depth_cm,
        total_forest_floor_depth_cm
      ),
      litter_load_mgha = finney_martin_cumulative_load(
        estimated_litter_depth_cm,
        total_forest_floor_depth_cm
      ),
      litter_load_raw_mgha = litter_load_mgha,
      litter_load_bounded_at_zero = litter_load_raw_mgha < 0,
      litter_load_mgha = pmax(litter_load_raw_mgha, 0),
      duff_load_mgha = total_forest_floor_load_mgha - litter_load_mgha
    )

  if (any(forest_floor_pre_station$duff_load_mgha < 0, na.rm = TRUE)) {
    stop(
      "Finney-Martin component calculation produced a negative duff load; inspect the input depths before proceeding."
    )
  }

  forest_floor_components <- forest_floor_pre_station |>
    select(phase, all_of(ids), station, litter_load_mgha, duff_load_mgha) |>
    pivot_longer(
      cols = ends_with("_load_mgha"),
      names_to = "component",
      values_to = "load_mgha"
    ) |>
    mutate(
      component = recode(
        component,
        litter_load_mgha = "litter",
        duff_load_mgha = "duff"
      ),
      derivation = "Finney-Martin 1993 model 3 cumulative-load partition"
    ) |>
    summarise(
      n_stations = sum(!is.na(load_mgha)),
      load_mgha = mean(load_mgha),
      derivation = first(derivation),
      .by = c(all_of(ids), "phase", "component")
    )
  saveRDS(
    forest_floor_station,
    file.path(paths$data, "forest-floor-measurements-station.rds")
  )
  saveRDS(
    forest_floor_pre_station,
    file.path(paths$data, "forest-floor-pre-components-station.rds")
  )
}

We’ll keep woody and herbacaceos vegetation separate, so herbaceous loads aren’t overwheled – they have very different implications for fire. We’ll convert cover and height using the thesis bulk densities, which used values from the firemon database manual, these should still be interpreted as operational convenience values rather than verified representative values for our systems. We’ll average the two stations within each transect. The displayed records show the loads and available station counts; a missing station leaves the transect mean missing. This review reads the combined component table saved in the next step.


Code
# f01-01-vegetation
if (recompute) {
  # FireMon-style vegetation calculations remain separate by physiognomic class.
  vegetation_station <- transects |>
    select(
      phase,
      all_of(ids),
      matches(
        "^(live_woody|dead_woody|avg_w_ht|live_herb|dead_herb|avg_h_ht)[12]$"
      )
    ) |>
    pivot_longer(
      cols = -c(phase, all_of(ids)),
      names_to = c(".value", "station"),
      names_pattern = "(.*?)([12])$"
    ) |>
    mutate(
      woody_height_m = if_else(live_woody == 0 & dead_woody == 0, 0, avg_w_ht),
      herb_height_m = if_else(live_herb == 0 & dead_herb == 0, 0, avg_h_ht),
      woody_load_mgha = ((live_woody + dead_woody) / 100) * woody_height_m * 18,
      herb_load_mgha = ((live_herb + dead_herb) / 100) * herb_height_m * 8
    ) |>
    select(phase, all_of(ids), station, woody_load_mgha, herb_load_mgha)

  vegetation_components <- vegetation_station |>
    pivot_longer(
      cols = ends_with("_load_mgha"),
      names_to = "component",
      values_to = "load_mgha"
    ) |>
    mutate(
      component = recode(
        component,
        woody_load_mgha = "woody_vegetation",
        herb_load_mgha = "herbaceous_vegetation"
      ),
      derivation = "FireMon cover-height bulk-density calculation retained by component"
    ) |>
    summarise(
      n_stations = sum(!is.na(load_mgha)),
      load_mgha = mean(load_mgha),
      derivation = first(derivation),
      .by = c("phase", all_of(ids), "component")
    )

To examine woody vegetation change, we need the two measurements from the same transect. We’ll match their identifiers before calculating pre-PCT minus post-PCT load. The pairing audit shows how many records can support that comparison and whether any are unmatched. This difference is an indicator of potential surface-fuel contribution; the measurements do not directly quantify deposited slash.


Code
# f01-01-pair-transects
if (recompute) {
  # Explicit pre/post joins replace the thesis-era lexical phase ordering used to
  # construct veg_diff. The primary PCT contrast is woody standing vegetation
  # reduction; it is an inferred surface-fuel contribution, not direct slash load.
  vegetation_wide <- fuel_components_transect |>
    filter(component %in% c("woody_vegetation", "herbaceous_vegetation")) |>
    select(all_of(ids), phase, component, load_mgha) |>
    pivot_wider(
      names_from = c(component, phase),
      values_from = load_mgha,
      names_sep = "_"
    )

  fuel_bed_depth_phase <- forest_floor_station |>
    summarise(
      n_fuel_bed_stations = sum(!is.na(fuel_bed_depth_cm)),
      fuel_bed_depth_cm = mean(fuel_bed_depth_cm),
      .by = c("phase", all_of(ids))
    ) |>
    pivot_wider(
      names_from = phase,
      values_from = c(fuel_bed_depth_cm, n_fuel_bed_stations),
      names_sep = "_"
    )

  fuel_paired_transect <- vegetation_wide |>
    filter(
      !is.na(woody_vegetation_prepct),
      !is.na(woody_vegetation_postpct)
    ) |>
    inner_join(fuel_bed_depth_phase, by = ids) |>
    mutate(
      woody_standing_reduction_mgha = woody_vegetation_prepct -
        woody_vegetation_postpct,
      herbaceous_vegetation_change_mgha = herbaceous_vegetation_postpct -
        herbaceous_vegetation_prepct,
      interpretation = "Woody standing-vegetation reduction is an inferred potential surface-fuel contribution; it is not a direct slash-load measurement."
    )

  pairing_qc <- bind_rows(
    transmute(
      distinct(
        filter(vegetation_wide, !is.na(woody_vegetation_prepct)),
        across(all_of(ids))
      ),
      status = "pre-PCT woody observation"
    ),
    transmute(
      distinct(
        filter(vegetation_wide, !is.na(woody_vegetation_postpct)),
        across(all_of(ids))
      ),
      status = "post-PCT woody observation"
    ),
    transmute(
      anti_join(
        distinct(
          filter(vegetation_wide, !is.na(woody_vegetation_prepct)),
          across(all_of(ids))
        ),
        distinct(
          filter(vegetation_wide, !is.na(woody_vegetation_postpct)),
          across(all_of(ids))
        ),
        by = ids
      ),
      status = "pre-PCT woody observation without post-PCT match"
    ),
    transmute(
      anti_join(
        distinct(
          filter(vegetation_wide, !is.na(woody_vegetation_postpct)),
          across(all_of(ids))
        ),
        distinct(
          filter(vegetation_wide, !is.na(woody_vegetation_prepct)),
          across(all_of(ids))
        ),
        by = ids
      ),
      status = "post-PCT woody observation without pre-PCT match"
    ),
    transmute(
      distinct(fuel_paired_transect, across(all_of(ids))),
      status = "matched woody pair"
    )
  ) |>
    count(status, name = "n_transects")
  saveRDS(
    fuel_paired_transect,
    file.path(paths$data, "fuel-paired-transect.rds")
  )
  write_csv(pairing_qc, file.path(paths$data, "fuel-pairing-qc.csv"))
}

text:
02 - Explore component distributions
Before choosing response distributions, we’ll look at how much the observed loads vary and how often a component is absent. The summaries below give means, spread, quantiles, zero counts, and missingness by phase, component, and treatment. Site, block, and corner counts show the available replication. These are raw descriptions of the transects; adjustment for the sampling hierarchy comes with the models later.


Code
# f01-02-explore-components
if (recompute) {
  publication_root <- normalizePath(getwd(), winslash = "/")
  paths_common <- publication_paths(publication_root)

  library(dplyr)
  library(readr)

  paths <- publication_fuel_paths(publication_root)
  components <- readRDS(file.path(paths$data, "fuel-components-transect.rds"))
  paired <- readRDS(file.path(paths$data, "fuel-paired-transect.rds"))

  add_design_groups <- function(data) {
    data |>
      mutate(
        block = interaction(site, treatment, drop = TRUE),
        design_corner = interaction(site, treatment, corner, drop = TRUE)
      )
  }

  component_data <- components |>
    mutate(component = as.character(component)) |>
    add_design_groups()

  component_summary <- component_data |>
    summarise(
      n_transects = n(),
      n_sites = n_distinct(site),
      n_blocks = n_distinct(block),
      n_corners = n_distinct(design_corner),
      n_zero = sum(load_mgha == 0, na.rm = TRUE),
      prop_zero = mean(load_mgha == 0, na.rm = TRUE),
      n_missing = sum(is.na(load_mgha)),
      mean_mgha = mean(load_mgha, na.rm = TRUE),
      sd_mgha = sd(load_mgha, na.rm = TRUE),
      variance_mgha = var(load_mgha, na.rm = TRUE),
      cv = if_else(mean_mgha > 0, sd_mgha / mean_mgha, NA_real_),
      min_mgha = min(load_mgha, na.rm = TRUE),
      q25_mgha = quantile(load_mgha, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE, names = FALSE),
      median_mgha = median(load_mgha, na.rm = TRUE),
      q75_mgha = quantile(load_mgha, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE, names = FALSE),
      max_mgha = max(load_mgha, na.rm = TRUE),
      .by = c("phase", "component", "treatment")
    ) |>
    arrange(phase, component, treatment)
  write_csv(
    component_summary,
    file.path(paths$data, "fuel-component-exploration-summary.csv")
  )
}

text:
03 - Fit phase-component candidates
We’ll now ask whether treatment differences in each component can be described with a common residual dispersion, or whether dispersion also needs to vary by treatment. Positive loads use Gamma models with a log link; components with zeros also get a zero submodel, with treatment-specific zero probabilities considered when there are at least eight zeros. The code defines these candidates and retains the additional site and dispersion alternatives for post-PCT 100-hour fuel.


Code
# f01-03-fit-phase-components
if (recompute) {
  # Preserve the fresh-Rscript RNG boundary of this historical fitting stage.
  # DHARMa 0.5.0 consumes an extra draw when .Random.seed is initially absent.
  if (exists(".Random.seed", envir = .GlobalEnv, inherits = FALSE)) {
    rm(".Random.seed", envir = .GlobalEnv)
  }
  publication_root <- normalizePath(getwd(), winslash = "/")
  paths_common <- publication_paths(publication_root)

  # Reuse the fitting functions defined above.

  library(dplyr)
  library(purrr)
  library(readr)

  paths <- publication_fuel_paths(publication_root)
  output_paths <- model_output_paths(paths)
  components <- readRDS(file.path(
    paths$data,
    "fuel-components-transect.rds"
  )) |>
    mutate(
      component = as.character(component),
      block = interaction(site, treatment, drop = TRUE),
      design_corner = interaction(site, treatment, corner, drop = TRUE)
    )

  design_formula <- load_mgha ~ treatment +
    (1 | site) +
    (1 | block) +
    (1 | design_corner)

  fit_component_candidates <- function(data, phase_value, component_value) {
    model_data <- data |>
      filter(
        .data$phase == .env$phase_value,
        .data$component == .env$component_value,
        !is.na(load_mgha)
      )
    zero_count <- sum(model_data$load_mgha == 0)
    prefix <- paste(phase_value, component_value, sep = "_")

    candidates <- list()
    if (zero_count > 0) {
      candidates[["base"]] <- list(
        family = glmmTMB::ziGamma(link = "log"),
        family_label = "ziGamma(link = log)",
        ziformula = ~1,
        dispformula = ~1
      )
      candidates[["disp_treatment"]] <- list(
        family = glmmTMB::ziGamma(link = "log"),
        family_label = "ziGamma(link = log)",
        ziformula = ~1,
        dispformula = ~treatment
      )
      if (zero_count >= 8) {
        candidates[["zi_treatment"]] <- list(
          family = glmmTMB::ziGamma(link = "log"),
          family_label = "ziGamma(link = log)",
          ziformula = ~treatment,
          dispformula = ~1
        )
      }
    } else {
      candidates[["base"]] <- list(
        family = Gamma(link = "log"),
        ziformula = ~0,
        dispformula = ~1
      )
      candidates[["disp_treatment"]] <- list(
        family = Gamma(link = "log"),
        ziformula = ~0,
        dispformula = ~treatment
      )
    }

    # The thesis used site plus treatment in both the zero and dispersion
    # submodels for post-PCT 100-hour fuels. Retain that candidate and add one
    # deliberately more complex site-by-treatment dispersion sensitivity check.
    if (phase_value == "postpct" && component_value == "hundhr") {
      candidates[["zi_treatment_site_disp_treatment_site"]] <- list(
        family = glmmTMB::ziGamma(link = "log"),
        family_label = "ziGamma(link = log)",
        ziformula = ~ treatment + site,
        dispformula = ~ treatment + site
      )
      candidates[["zi_treatment_site_disp_treatment_site_interaction"]] <- list(
        family = glmmTMB::ziGamma(link = "log"),
        family_label = "ziGamma(link = log)",
        ziformula = ~ treatment + site,
        dispformula = ~ treatment * site
      )
    }

    imap_dfr(candidates, function(candidate, candidate_name) {
      fit_and_diagnose(
        simulation_n = 1000,
        simulation_seed = 20260918,
        model_id = paste(prefix, candidate_name, sep = "_"),
        response = component_value,
        analysis = paste(phase_value, "phase-specific component", sep = ": "),
        data = model_data,
        formula = design_formula,
        family = candidate$family,
        family_label = candidate$family_label,
        ziformula = candidate$ziformula,
        dispformula = candidate$dispformula,
        paths = paths
      )
    })
  }
}

text:
04 - Fit matched woody candidates
Without a defensible post-PCT slash-depth conversion, the change in standing woody load offers one way to explore PCT’s potential contribution to surface fuels. We’ll compare a model of the paired differences with a joint model of the two phases. Woody loads are nonnegative, include zeros, and can be strongly right-skewed. A difference between two such loads can be negative, zero, or positive, with a distribution unlike either phase alone. Modeling the loads jointly respects their original scale and supplies both phase estimates. Modeling the observed differences directly asks whether a simpler change response gives a defensible account of the same paired data. These alternatives test different distributional and variance assumptions; they do not change the definition of woody reduction.
For transect \(i\), the observed signed difference is \(d_i = y_{i,\mathrm{pre}} - y_{i,\mathrm{post}}\). Positive values indicate less standing woody vegetation after PCT; negative values indicate more. Here, “signed-difference model” means fitting \(d_i\) directly, while “contrast from the joint phase model” means subtracting its two fitted response-scale means. Both yield signed changes in Mg/ha; a contrast is a derived quantity, not a separate response family.








Feature
Joint phase model and derived contrast
Direct signed-difference model




Response
Two woody loads per matched transect, one per phase.
One observed pre-minus-post difference per matched transect.


Treatment effects
phase * treatment allows phase change to vary by treatment.
treatment allows the difference to vary by treatment.


Distribution
A zero probability plus a Gamma distribution for positive loads, with a log link.
Gaussian or Student-t with an identity link, allowing either sign.


Pairing and design
Site, block, and corner random intercepts, plus a shared transect intercept linking the two phases.
Pairing is already used in the subtraction; site, block, and corner random intercepts retain clustering among differences.


Available estimates
Pre- and post-PCT mean loads and their covariance-aware difference.
Treatment-specific differences; the two phase means cannot be recovered from differences alone.



For the joint model, RD04 derives \(\Delta_t = \mu_{\mathrm{pre},t} - \mu_{\mathrm{post},t}\) from means that include the zero probability and integrate over the fitted random effects, with equal study-site weights. Exponentiating a phase contrast on the log scale would instead give a ratio in the positive-load submodel. The uncertainty of the response-scale difference retains the covariance between the estimated phase means: \(\operatorname{Var}(\hat\Delta_t) =
\operatorname{Var}(\hat\mu_{\mathrm{pre},t}) +
\operatorname{Var}(\hat\mu_{\mathrm{post},t}) -
2\operatorname{Cov}(\hat\mu_{\mathrm{pre},t},\hat\mu_{\mathrm{post},t})\). The direct model represents paired change through the distribution of \(d_i\) itself. Although \(E(Y_{\mathrm{pre}}-Y_{\mathrm{post}}) =
E(Y_{\mathrm{pre}})-E(Y_{\mathrm{post}})\) when the means exist, separately fitted models need not give identical estimates or intervals because their assumptions and use of the phase information differ.
The three joint candidates use a common zero probability and dispersion, a phase-specific zero probability, or phase-specific dispersion. These distinguish changes in the frequency of absent woody vegetation from changes in the spread of positive loads. The six direct candidates use Gaussian errors with common or treatment-specific dispersion, or Student-t errors with common, treatment, additive treatment-plus-site, or treatment-by-site dispersion. Student-t provides heavier tails for unusually large changes; the dispersion alternatives assess whether residual spread differs among treatments and sites. No zero-inflation submodel is used for the signed response: a zero difference means equal phase loads, not necessarily absent woody vegetation. The family and submodel definitions follow the glmmTMB family documentation and fitting documentation.
The current saved fits use 234 phase-load observations or 117 paired differences. Their likelihoods describe different responses, so AIC is compared within each approach, not across the two approaches, following the same-data requirement for AIC. Convergence and residual checks still determine what needs follow-up. RD04 uses the joint model so its displayed woody change agrees with its phase means; the direct models remain sensitivity candidates. Neither approach establishes a causal PCT effect or measures slash production directly.
The cell below fits both candidate sets and brings all nine attempts into one register. We’ll use its convergence and residual fields to assess the alternatives alongside AIC within each approach. Diagnostics use 1,000 unconditional DHARMa simulations with seed 20260918; recompute reads saved models, refit replaces them, and an ordinary render shows the saved register.


Code
# f01-04-fit-woody-pct-models
if (recompute) {
  # This stage formerly started in a separate Rscript process. Restore its empty
  # initial RNG state; the diagnostic seed and unconditional simulations are unchanged.
  if (exists(".Random.seed", envir = .GlobalEnv, inherits = FALSE)) {
    rm(".Random.seed", envir = .GlobalEnv)
  }
  publication_root <- normalizePath(getwd(), winslash = "/")
  paths_common <- publication_paths(publication_root)

  # Reuse the fitting functions defined above.

  library(dplyr)
  library(readr)
  library(tidyr)

  paths <- publication_fuel_paths(publication_root)
  output_paths <- model_output_paths(paths)
  paired <- readRDS(file.path(paths$data, "fuel-paired-transect.rds")) |>
    mutate(
      block = interaction(site, treatment, drop = TRUE),
      design_corner = interaction(site, treatment, corner, drop = TRUE),
      transect_id = interaction(site, treatment, corner, azi, drop = TRUE)
    )

  woody_long <- paired |>
    select(
      site,
      treatment,
      corner,
      azi,
      block,
      design_corner,
      transect_id,
      woody_vegetation_prepct,
      woody_vegetation_postpct

      names_prefix = "woody_vegetation_",
      values_to = "load_mgha"
    ) |>
    mutate(phase = factor(phase, levels = c("prepct", "postpct")))

    (1 | site) +
    (1 | block) +
    (1 | design_corner) +

  # Model the paired phase loads; RD04 derives their response-scale contrast.

    fit_and_diagnose(
      simulation_n = 1000,
      simulation_seed = 20260918,
      model_id = "woody_phase_zigamma_zi1_disp1",

    fit_and_diagnose(

      simulation_seed = 20260918,
      model_id = "woody_phase_zigamma_ziphase_disp1",
      response = "woody vegetation load",
      analysis = "matched repeated-measures phase model",
      data = woody_long,
      formula = phase_formula,
      family = glmmTMB::ziGamma(link = "log"),
      family_label = "ziGamma(link = log)",
      ziformula = ~phase,
      dispformula = ~1,
      paths = paths
    ),
    fit_and_diagnose(
      simulation_n = 1000,
      simulation_seed = 20260918,
      model_id = "woody_phase_zigamma_zi1_dispphase",
      response = "woody vegetation load",
      analysis = "matched repeated-measures phase model",
      data = woody_long,
      formula = phase_formula,
      family = glmmTMB::ziGamma(link = "log"),
      family_label = "ziGamma(link = log)",
      ziformula = ~1,
      dispformula = ~phase,
      paths = paths
    )
  )

  # Model each transect's observed signed difference directly.
  delta_formula <- woody_standing_reduction_mgha ~ treatment +
    (1 | site) +
    (1 | block) +
    (1 | design_corner)

  delta_registry <- bind_rows(
    fit_and_diagnose(
      simulation_n = 1000,
      simulation_seed = 20260918,
      model_id = "woody_delta_gaussian",
      response = "woody standing-vegetation reduction",
      analysis = "signed matched pre-minus-post contrast",
      data = paired,
      formula = delta_formula,
      family = gaussian(),
      family_label = "Gaussian(identity)",
      ziformula = ~0,
      dispformula = ~1,
      paths = paths
    ),
    fit_and_diagnose(
      simulation_n = 1000,
      simulation_seed = 20260918,
      model_id = "woody_delta_gaussian_disp_treatment",
      response = "woody standing-vegetation reduction",
      analysis = "signed matched pre-minus-post contrast",
      data = paired,
      formula = delta_formula,
      family = gaussian(),
      family_label = "Gaussian(identity)",
      ziformula = ~0,
      dispformula = ~treatment,
      paths = paths
    ),
    fit_and_diagnose(
      simulation_n = 1000,
      simulation_seed = 20260918,
      model_id = "woody_delta_student_t",
      response = "woody standing-vegetation reduction",
      analysis = "signed matched pre-minus-post contrast",
      data = paired,
      formula = delta_formula,
      family = glmmTMB::t_family(),
      family_label = "Student-t(identity)",
      ziformula = ~0,
      dispformula = ~1,
      paths = paths
    ),
    fit_and_diagnose(
      simulation_n = 1000,
      simulation_seed = 20260918,
      model_id = "woody_delta_student_t_disp_treatment",
      response = "woody standing-vegetation reduction",

      data = paired,

      simulation_n = 1000,
      simulation_seed = 20260918,

      response = "woody standing-vegetation reduction",
      analysis = "signed matched pre-minus-post contrast",
      data = paired,
      formula = delta_formula,
      family = glmmTMB::t_family(),
      family_label = "Student-t(identity)",

    ),

      simulation_n = 1000,
      simulation_seed = 20260918,

How does regeneration basal area differ among the retained-overstory treatments, and how sensitive is that pattern to the way we represent species and sampling groups? text:
Integrated means and uncertainty
To compare models meaningfully, we need their estimates to describe the same quantity: arithmetic expected basal area, including plots where a species is absent. We’ll define a shared calculation that includes modeled zeros and integrates over independent Gaussian random intercepts. Its intervals carry the full parameter covariance, including uncertainty in random-effect variances. The later estimate tables use this calculation, checked against numerical predictions, derivatives, and quadrature.


Code
# rd02-integrated-means
integrated_means <- function(m, id, species = NULL) {
  stopifnot(m$fit$convergence == 0, m$sdr$pdHess)
  frame <- model.frame(m)
  if (!"spp" %in% names(frame)) frame$spp <- species
  grid <- distinct(frame, site, treat, spp, .keep_all = TRUE)
  labels <- distinct(grid, treat, spp)
  A <- t(vapply(seq_len(nrow(labels)), function(i) {
    keep <- grid$treat == labels$treat[i] & grid$spp == labels$spp[i]
    as.numeric(keep) / sum(keep)
  }, numeric(nrow(grid))))
  stopifnot(all(rowSums(A > 0) == 4L), family(m)$link == "log",
            length(VarCorr(m)$zi) == 0L,
            all(vapply(VarCorr(m)$cond, function(v) identical(dim(v), c(1L, 1L)), logical(1))))
  X <- model.matrix(delete.response(terms(formula(m, fixed.only = TRUE))), grid)
  Z <- model.matrix(formula(m, component = "zi", fixed.only = TRUE), grid)
  b <- m$fit$par
  ib <- which(names(b) == "beta")
  iz <- which(names(b) == "betazi")
  it <- which(names(b) == "theta")
  stopifnot(identical(colnames(X), names(fixef(m)$cond)),
            identical(colnames(Z), names(fixef(m)$zi)),
            length(it) == length(VarCorr(m)$cond),
            isTRUE(all.equal(unname(b), unname(m$sdr$par.fixed))))
  variance <- sum(exp(2 * b[it]))
  pzero <- plogis(drop(Z %*% b[iz]))
  mu <- exp(drop(X %*% b[ib]) + variance / 2) * (1 - pzero)
  D <- matrix(0, nrow(grid), length(b))
  D[, ib] <- mu * X
  D[, iz] <- -mu * pzero * Z
  D[, it] <- outer(mu, exp(2 * b[it]))
  G <- A %*% D
  estimate <- drop(A %*% mu)
  se <- sqrt(diag(G %*% m$sdr$cov.fixed %*% t(G)))
  functional <- function(b) drop(A %*% (
    exp(drop(X %*% b[ib]) + sum(exp(2 * b[it])) / 2) *
      (1 - plogis(drop(Z %*% b[iz])))))
  numeric_G <- numDeriv::jacobian(functional, unname(b))
  quadrature <- integrate(function(z) exp(sqrt(variance) * z) * dnorm(z), -12, 12)$value
  stopifnot(max(abs(G - numeric_G) / pmax(1, abs(G))) < 1e-5,
            max(abs(mu / exp(variance / 2) - predict(m, grid, type = "response", re.form = NA))) < 1e-7,
            abs(quadrature - exp(variance / 2)) < 1e-8,
            all(is.finite(se)), all(se > 0),
            abs(sum(vapply(VarCorr(m)$cond, function(v) v[1, 1], numeric(1))) - variance) < 1e-9)
  mutate(labels, model_id = id, estimate = estimate, se = se,
    lcl = estimate * exp(-qnorm(.975) * se / estimate),
    ucl = estimate * exp(qnorm(.975) * se / estimate),
    total_random_variance = variance, integration_multiplier = exp(variance / 2))
}

    records[[id]] <- data.frame(
      model_id = id, formula = paste(deparse(formulas[[id]]), collapse = " "),
      n = nobs(fit), k = attr(ll, "df"), log_likelihood = as.numeric(ll),
      AIC = AIC(fit), BIC = BIC(fit), convergence = fit$fit$convergence,
      pd_hessian = fit$sdr$pdHess,
      max_abs_gradient = max(abs(fit$sdr$gradient.fixed)),
      min_random_sd = min(variance_records[[id]]$sd),
      near_boundary_sd_lt_1e_3 = any(variance_records[[id]]$sd < 1e-3),
      warnings = paste(unique(fit_warnings), collapse = " | ")
    )
    # glmmTMB's simulation in this installed version draws new random effects.
    # Explicitly record the version and use the same seed and n for all models.
    sim <- publication_simulate_residuals(fit, n = simulations, seed = seed, refit = FALSE, plot = FALSE)
    saveRDS(sim, file.path(out, "models", paste0(id, "-dharma.rds")))
    diagnostic_records[[id]] <- test_record(sim, id, "species_plot_rows")
    # Recalculate residuals on aggregated responses to inspect each design level.
    groups <- list(site = d$site, macro_plot = interaction(d$site, d$treat, drop = TRUE),
                   vegetation_plot = interaction(d$site, d$treat, d$plot, drop = TRUE))
    for (scope in names(groups)) {
      grouped <- recalculateResiduals(sim, group = groups[[scope]], seed = seed)
      diagnostic_records[[id]] <- bind_rows(diagnostic_records[[id]], test_record(grouped, id, scope))
    }
    png(file.path(out, "diagnostics", paste0(id, "-dharma.png")),
        width = 1800, height = 1000, res = 160)
    plot(sim)
    dev.off()
    png(file.path(out, "diagnostics", paste0(id, "-by-species-treatment.png")),
        width = 1800, height = 1000, res = 160)
    old_par <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
    plotResiduals(sim, form = d$spp)
    plotResiduals(sim, form = d$treat)
    par(old_par)
    dev.off()
  }
  comparison <- bind_rows(records) |>
    mutate(delta_AIC = AIC - min(AIC[convergence == 0 & pd_hessian], na.rm = TRUE))
  variance_table <- bind_rows(variance_records)
  diagnostics <- bind_rows(diagnostic_records)
  write.csv(comparison, file.path(out, "tables/rd02-model-comparison.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
  write.csv(variance_table, file.path(out, "tables/rd02-random-effect-variances.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
  write.csv(diagnostics, file.path(out, "tables/rd02-dharma-tests.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
}

A variance estimate near zero could reflect little detectable variation at that level or difficulty locating the optimum. We’ll check the design-model fits with BFGS, starting random-effect SDs at 0.3. The table reports whether the objective agrees within 1e-4, helping us assess whether the boundary estimates depend on the fitting route.

# rd02-02-optimizer
if (recompute) {
  # Boundary components warrant an optimizer/start sensitivity check. Start each
  # random SD at 0.3 rather than inheriting the near-zero nlminb estimates.
  optimizer_checks <- bind_rows(lapply(c("full_nested", "nested_plus_site_species"), function(id) {
    message("Checking BFGS optimizer/start sensitivity: ", id)
    warnings <- character()
    check <- if (isTRUE(params$refit)) {
  withCallingHandlers(update(models[[id]],
      start = list(theta = rep(log(.3), sum(names(models[[id]]$fit$par) == "theta"))),
      control = glmmTMBControl(optimizer = optim, optArgs = list(method = "BFGS"),
                              optCtrl = list(maxit = 10000, reltol = 1e-10))),
      warning = function(w) {

    } else {

    }
    if (isTRUE(params$refit)) saveRDS(check, file.path(out, "models", paste0(id, "-bfgs.rds")))

  write.csv(optimizer_checks, file.path(out, "tables/rd02-optimizer-sensitivity.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
}

The historical model’s residual check flagged the tails, so we’ll examine whether that signal persists with 10,000 simulations and another seed. The repeated tests and flagged rows below show how sensitive the finding is to simulation. We retain every observation while investigating the flag.

# rd02-02-tail-check
if (recompute) {
  # Inspect the baseline tail flag without removing observations or changing the
  # fit. More simulations and a second seed check Monte Carlo sensitivity.
  tail_check <- publication_simulate_residuals(models$thesis_site_species, n = 10000,
                                  seed = seed + 1L, refit = FALSE, plot = FALSE)
  tail_tests <- test_record(tail_check, "thesis_site_species", "species_plot_rows_10000_simulations")
  write.csv(tail_tests, file.path(out, "tables/rd02-baseline-tail-sensitivity.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

      tail_check$scaledResiduals
    d |>

      filter(dharma_residual < 1 / (n + 1) | dharma_residual > 1 - 1 / (n + 1))
  }))
  write.csv(tail_rows, file.path(out, "tables/rd02-baseline-tail-observations.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
}

Do the alternative clustering assumptions change the treatment means enough to matter for the regeneration story? We’ll calculate integrated means and full-covariance intervals for each converged joint model. The tables show the estimates and their changes from the historical structure, with common zero and dispersion specifications so the comparison focuses on random-effect structure.
